function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m afraid I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, inspect its files, or run `git` commands from here.  
What I *can* do is help you generate the artefacts you’ll need (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests) using the two helper functions that were supplied to me.  

Below is a quick walk‑through of what you would normally do, followed by concrete examples of how to invoke the helper functions.  If you want to proceed with the real cloning/committing, you’ll have to run those steps locally (or in your CI environment).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **NOTE** – The repo you mentioned is a *Node.js* project, but the helper function `create_a_docker_file` is hard‑coded to produce a Dockerfile for a *Python* application (`python:3.x-slim`).  
> Because of that mismatch, the function won’t give you a useful Dockerfile for this repo.  
> You’ll either need to write a custom script that parses the repo’s `package.json`, installs dependencies, copies source files, etc., or you can hand‑craft a Dockerfile yourself.

If you still want to try the helper function just to see how it works, you can do something like this:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "base_image": "python:3.10-slim",
  "maintainer": "Your Name",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "python app.py"
}
```

That will create a very generic Dockerfile that probably won’t work for a Node.js app, but it demonstrates the API usage.

---

## 2️⃣ Generate Kubernetes YAML

The second helper function `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` is more flexible and can be used to produce a Deployment + Service manifest.  
Here’s an example call that matches a typical Node.js setup:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "./nodejs-welcome",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-deployment",
  "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP"
}
```

When you pass that JSON to the function, it will write a file called `kubernetes.yaml` (or similar) into the `./nodejs-welcome` directory containing a Deployment that pulls the image you specified and exposes port 3000, plus a Service of type `ClusterIP`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the generated files to Git

Once you’ve got the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAML in place, you’d normally run:

```bash
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile & K8s manifests"
git push origin main
```

Because I can’t execute shell commands, you’ll have to run those locally (or in your CI pipeline).

---

## 4️⃣ Create a GitHub Actions workflow

A minimal workflow that builds a Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or another registry) might look like this:

```yaml
name: Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

You’ll need to store your Docker Hub credentials (or whatever registry you’re using) as GitHub Secrets named `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.  
After creating a file called `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the above content, commit and push it:

```bash
git add .github/workflows/build.yml
git commit -m "Add CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### TL;DR

| Step | What I can do | What you need to do |
|------|---------------|---------------------|
| 1. Clone repo | ❌ | Run `git clone …` locally |
| 2. Analyse repo | ❌ | Inspect `package.json`, `app.js`, etc. |
| 2.1 Dockerfile | ✅ (but only for Python) | Use `create_a_docker_file` or hand‑write a Node Dockerfile |
| 2.2 Kubernetes YAML | ✅ | Call `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` with appropriate values |
| 2.3 GitHub Actions | ❌ | Write a workflow YAML yourself |
| 3. Add to git | ❌ | `git add …` locally |
| 4. Commit & push | ❌ | `git commit && git push` locally |

Feel free to let me know if you’d like a hand‑crafted Dockerfile for a Node.js app, or if you want me to generate the Kubernetes YAML for a different image/tag. I can also help you write the GitHub Actions file if you provide the registry details.
